1.28.2.en: Whoever listens to the voice of wisdom, preferring it to the enticements of the wicked, dwells safely, that is, he comes to be in complete safety, and is quiet from fear of evil, enjoying the wealth of the righteousness of Christ and His protection of him.

1.28.3.en: * What is truly good is seen to be delightful, and produces tasty fruit: tranquility of soul!

1.28.4.en: It is said: “But whoso hearkeneth unto me shall dwell safely, and shall be quiet from fear of evil” [33]. “Trust in God with all thy heart, and all thy mind upon God.”

1.28.5.en: St. Clement of Alexandria * “And we desire that every one of you do shew the same diligence to the full assurance of hope unto the end... Whither the forerunner is for us entered, even Jesus, made an high priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec” (Heb 6: 11-20). In the same way Paul the Apostle, full of wisdom, says: “But whoso hearkeneth unto me shall dwell safely, trusting in hope”..

1.28.6.en: To the expression “dwell” the word “trusting” was beautifully added, showing that whoever receives rest enjoys hope in what he hopes for; therefore it was added: “and shall be quiet from fear of evil.”

2.0.0.en: 1 My son, if thou wilt receive my words, and hide my commandments with thee; 2 So that thou incline thine ear unto wisdom, and apply thine heart to understanding; 3 Yea, if thou criest after knowledge, and liftest up thy voice for understanding; 4 If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures; 5 Then shalt thou understand the fear of the LORD, and find the knowledge of God. 6 For the LORD giveth wisdom: out of his mouth cometh knowledge and understanding. 7 He layeth up help for the upright: he is a buckler to them that walk uprightly. 8 He keepeth the paths of judgment, and preserveth the way of his saints. 9 Then shalt thou understand righteousness, and judgment, and equity; yea, every good path.

2.0.1.en: In this passage [1-9] Solomon the Wise speaks with the believer as with his spiritual son, urging him to listen to the word of God which he utters, to hide it as a treasure in his depths, to incline his ear to it, and to open his heart to it so that it may settle in him. By this he enjoys the fear of the Lord and receives the knowledge of God, is fortified with the spiritual weapons of God, and walks the upright royal way.

2.0.2.en: “My son, if thou wilt receive my words, and hide my commandments with thee...” [1].

2.0.3.en: “Solomon” speaks as a teacher with his disciple, reckoning him his son, since he offers him his heart full of love together with a word of teaching. And St. Clement of Alexandria says: “Every person who learns submits to his teacher as a son.”

2.0.4.en: Would that before we offer our words to others we offered our hearts full of love for them, and aflame with true longing for their salvation and glory.

2.0.5.en: The father asks his son to receive his words and to hide his commandments. This is the first lesson in the school of this life, which is the son’s acceptance of and response to the words of his parents. It is as though he answers sincere fatherly love with practical filial love. Not only that he respond to him, but that he hide it in his heart with all care and concern as the most precious and best of treasures. The living believer stands from time to time looking toward his inner treasure, contemplating the treasures he has acquired and stored up, admiring them as divine gifts at work in his daily life.

2.0.6.en: Solomon the Wise counsels us to hide the commandments of the parents, those which are without doubt in complete harmony with the commandments of the Holy Bible. We hide them in our hearts, so that when we fulfill them our conduct proceeds mingled with the inner feelings of the heart, and we fulfill them with our full freedom and great joy, and not like one who practices them under compulsion, as one fulfilling a duty he is bound to. Whoever puts the commandment in his heart fulfills it with his heart, and his heart accompanies him wherever he goes, and so he finds his delight in the will of his heavenly Father.

2.0.7.en: The believer hides in his heart the commandment of God, his precious treasure, the most precious thing in his life, the center of love and life, and the place of safety, so that the enemy cannot break in upon him to seize it from him. We hide the commandment of God, and then no sin can hide in the heart or creep into it, for darkness cannot find a place where light is. Perhaps the wise man asks us to hide the commandment in our heart so that we may meditate on it and be occupied with it, and our spiritual stomach digest it. For just as food that is not digested does not benefit the body at all, so whoever hears the commandment and does not meditate on it and occupy himself with it, his soul does not benefit from it.

2.0.8.en: Anthimus, bishop of Jerusalem, gives three reasons for hiding the word of God in the heart:

2.0.9.en: [A - He hides the word of God in his heart who is warned against error, not only in outward action but also in hidden thought. Such a one avoids not only fornication but also the perversion of his desire and its hidden inclination...

2.0.10.en: B - And also he who hides in his heart the mysteries of the faith and does not disclose them to unbelievers, acting by His saying: “Neither cast ye your pearls before swine.”

2.0.11.en: C - Likewise he who hides the sayings of God in his heart lest the birds of the air snatch them, I mean by them the demons fallen from heaven, so that they do not rob him of them by doubt or pride or evil thought...]

2.0.12.en: * He who does not receive the teachings of God superficially and outwardly but hides them in his heart until his thought and also his intentions are set straight, becomes free of sin before God, who sees what is hidden, for he commits not only adultery but also every evil desire. This verse corresponds to the words: “My son, if thou wilt receive my words, and hide my commandments with thee, so that thou incline thine ear unto wisdom” (Prov 2:1, 2).

2.0.13.en: St. Didymus the Blind * If we do not hide the sayings of God in our heart as we hide a jewel, the wicked one comes and snatches it (Mt 13:19).

2.1.0.en: St. Athanasius the Apostolic * He asked first for divine help, lest the words of God hidden in his heart be hidden without fruit, where works of righteousness do not follow them. Therefore after saying this he added: “Blessed art thou, O Lord, teach me thy righteousness” [12].

2.1.1.en: Because I have hidden Your words in my heart so that I might not sin against You, who gave me the Law, grant me also the blessing of Your grace, so that by doing what is upright I may learn what You have commanded...

2.1.2.en: St. Augustine It is good for a person to study the Holy Bible with the aid of some study references and commentaries, but there is no book that can take the place of the word of God. Therefore it is fitting for the believer to have his quiet sitting with the word of God, asking God to let him taste it in his depths so that he may live it in his daily life wherever he is.

2.1.3.en: Relying on previous studies is beneficial, especially the writings of the Fathers on the Holy Bible, since their lives were an open practical Gospel; but if a person does not meet the Word personally, these studies become dry, without renewed spiritual fruit.

2.1.4.en: “So that thou incline thine ear unto wisdom, and apply thine heart to understanding; Yea, if thou criest after knowledge, and liftest up thy voice for understanding” [2, 3].

2.1.5.en: The wise man urges us to devote all the senses of the body and its members, together with the soul, to seeking to learn wisdom, knowledge and understanding. This is what we seek with all our energies, listen to, and carry into our hearts. We incline our ears, open our hearts and cry with our tongues until the wisdom of God enters into our depths, into the mind as into the heart. She grants us understanding and satisfies our hearts.

2.1.6.en: Let us cry to God with our tongues as with our inner voices, for God is pleased with the cries of the heart, and He alone is the giver of wisdom. The Apostle Peter expressed the longing of believers for divine wisdom, saying: “As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby” (1 Pet 3:2). When the baby sees his mother preparing the bottle of milk he moves with all the members of his body, with his tongue and hands and feet and head, etc., to express his desire to nurse. So we, as children of God, declare our eagerness for the milk of the Word, crying out to Him.

2.1.7.en: Prayer, especially for the enjoyment of divine knowledge, is the language of the soul’s longing toward God. It is the interpreter of the heart’s yearning. Therefore St. Augustine distinguishes between one who offers by his prayer a voice and one who offers a meaningless noise. He says that when we pray without love our prayers are a noise in which God has no pleasure. On the contrary, He is pleased with the prayer that carries a meaningful voice, since it carries love with it. Therefore the psalmist often uses the expression “voice” when speaking of prayer:

2.1.8.en: “I cried unto the LORD with my voice” (Ps 3:4).

2.1.9.en: “My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD” (Ps 5:3).

2.1.10.en: “And he heard my voice out of his temple” (Ps 18:6).

2.1.11.en: “With my voice I call; therefore have mercy upon me” (Ps 27:7).

2.1.13.en: “Attend to the voice of my prayer” (Ps 66: 19).

2.1.14.en: * Who can doubt that the cries raised to the Lord in the sound of prayer are in vain if they are uttered with the voice of the body and not with the voice of the heart that is fixed in God?!

2.1.15.en: But if they proceed from the heart they escape the notice of men, if through bodily weakness the person is silent, yet they do not escape the notice of God. Therefore when we cry to the Lord with the voice of the body, where circumstances require it, or in silence, we must cry from the heart.

2.1.16.en: * He says “the voice of my prayer” (Ps 140:7); that is, the life of my prayer, or the soul of my prayer, and not merely the sounds of my words, but what gives the words life. For every other noise that has no life can be called sounds and not words.

2.1.17.en: Words belong to those who have souls, that is, to the living; but how do many pray to God while they have no understanding worthy of God and no upright thoughts toward Him? Such people may have the sound of prayer but cannot have the intelligible voice, because there is no life in their prayers.

2.1.18.en: * The cry to God is not made with a bodily voice but with the heart. Many have silent lips yet cry out with the heart, and many offer noise with their lips while their hearts have become unable to offer anything. Therefore if you cry to God, cry to Him from within, where He hears you.

2.1.19.en: * The mouth speaks through the mediation of words; and the heart speaks through the mediation of its desires. Your prayer is the desire of your heart.

2.1.20.en: * God does not seek words but your hearts.

2.1.21.en: * With the heart we ask, with the heart we seek, and at the voice of the heart the door is opened.

2.1.22.en: * He who prays with desire praises in his heart even if his tongue is silent. But if (a person) prays without longing he is dumb before God even if his voice reaches the ears of men.

2.1.23.en: St. Augustine “If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures” [4].

2.1.24.en: The search for wisdom is compared to the search for silver and other precious metals in deep mines. Wisdom, like these treasures, is not found by chance by a passer-by, but the matter requires enormous efforts and discovery and digging. So it is fitting for us to search for the salvation of our souls with burning zeal, as the lover of money searches for wealth. And we should be ashamed of ourselves if our longing for salvation and for the enjoyment of wisdom as true wealth is less than our search for the wealth of the world. Let us search for wisdom with unparalleled diligence, burning desire and great patience.

2.1.25.en: It is noticed that the word “treasures” here means the possession of what is hidden in the earth and in caves, and it can also mean the precious metals and precious stones found in mines. How do we seek them? By digging the mines until we reach them in the bowels of the earth.

2.1.26.en: * God does not want us to listen to the words and phrases in the Holy Bible carelessly, but with great attention. This is what moved the blessed David to put the title “for understanding” in many places of his psalms. As he says: “Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law” (Ps 119: 18, 130). And after him his son also came to show the necessity of seeking wisdom as silver, and of trading in it as more precious than gold (Prov 2:4; 3:14) [He also quoted: “Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me” Jn 5:39]. When the Lord urges the Jews to search the scriptures, He urges us all the more to search. For He would not have said this if it were possible to grasp the scriptures completely as soon as we read them. No one searches for what is plain and in his hands, but he searches for what is hidden in shadow, which we must find by searching. So, to urge us to search, He calls it “the hid treasure” (Prov 2:4; Mt 13:44). These words were said to us so that we may not apply the words of Scripture slackly or carelessly, but with great precision. For if someone listens to what is said in the Scriptures without searching for the spiritual meaning but accepts the literal meaning, he thinks things unworthy of God, such as that He is wrathful and furious, and what is worse than this.

2.1.27.en: St. John Chrysostom “Then shalt thou understand the fear of the LORD, and find the knowledge of God. For the LORD giveth wisdom: out of his mouth cometh knowledge and understanding.

2.1.28.en: He layeth up help for the upright.

2.1.29.en: He is a buckler to them that walk uprightly” [5-7].

2.1.30.en: In the Book of Proverbs Solomon the Wise affirms the close relationship between wisdom and the fear of the Lord. We have already seen that the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and at the same time whoever attains understanding and enjoys knowledge and wisdom perceives the fear of the Lord and touches it practically. The fear of the Lord is not the motto of the Book of Proverbs alone, but the motto of the whole Holy Bible. St. Ambrose says that the house of wisdom can be built only if the fear of God is deeply established in the soul.

2.1.31.en: The search for truth must always be accompanied by a walk in the truth that we find. By this God gives His godly ones renewed concepts of the truth, and an ever-increasing living experience of the power of truth.

2.1.32.en: * I want to have a fitting fear founded on reason and understanding... so that we may not have fear without understanding, nor understanding without fear.

2.1.33.en: Origen sees Solomon the Wise as saying that wisdom proceeds as though from the mouth of God to be directed toward the ears of the believer, and goes out to his heart as to his mind, and there it settles, where his will, his senses and his feelings, and therefore his words and his conduct, are sanctified.

2.1.34.en: God is the fountain of all wisdom, knowledge and understanding, and the truly wise and understanding are channels through which God pours out wisdom on many. Divine wisdom is a buckler for the people of God who walk uprightly, or a help for them to obtain victory. For as we hold fast to wisdom and keep her, she holds fast to us and keeps us.

2.1.35.en: * For those who are justified by philosophy, knowledge leads them to godliness as a help for them.

2.1.36.en: St. Clement of Alexandria Origen comments on what is in the Septuagint: “They shall find a divine sense” for the Hebrew text: “and find the knowledge of God” [5], explaining that just as the body has its own senses for temporal things, so the soul of the believer enjoys divine senses that concern heavenly things.

2.1.37.en: * To learn from the Holy Scriptures that there is a divine sense other than the senses of the body, read only what Solomon the Wise says: “Thou shalt find a divine sense” [5].

2.1.38.en: * Lest it be thought that our saying that rational things are not known by the senses is unsound, Solomon the Wise used an example, for he says: “Thou shalt find also a divine sense,” showing by this that these rational things are not sought by a bodily sense, but by another particular sense which he calls “divine.” It is fitting for us to look through this sense at every one of the rational beings that we reckon to be heavenly. By this sense the words we utter are understood, and by it our phrases which we write are weighed. For the divine nature knows those thoughts that go on within us while we are silent.

2.1.39.en: * (Solomon) knew that there are two kinds of senses within us: mortal senses, which can be corrupted and are human, and the others immortal and rational, which he calls “divine.”

2.1.40.en: By this divine sense, not the sense of the two eyes but the sense of the pure heart, which is the mind, God is seen by those who are worthy of it. For certainly you will find in all the Holy Scriptures, old and new, the expression “heart” repeated in place of “mind,” that is, the rational faculty.

2.1.41.en: Origen St. Augustine comments on the phrase “out of his mouth (face) cometh knowledge and understanding” [6], saying:

2.1.42.en: * True faith and sound teaching declare that both graces are from God. The Holy Bible says: “Out of his face cometh knowledge and understanding,” and in another book it says: “Love is of God” (1 Jn 4:7).

2.1.43.en: * “For the LORD giveth wisdom: out of his mouth cometh knowledge and understanding” [6]. From Him they receive the very desire for knowledge, when it is joined (wedded) to godliness.

2.1.44.en: St. Augustine “He layeth up help for the upright: he is a buckler to them that walk uprightly.

2.1.45.en: He keepeth the paths of judgment, and preserveth the way of his saints” [7, 8].

2.1.46.en: God Himself keeps the paths of judgment, which are the paths of His righteousness, so that His believers may walk in them under His care and protection. And it is He who preserves the way of His saints who keep their covenant with Him. It is as though God, who grants wisdom, knowledge and understanding, also gives victory to His believers and protects them as they walk in His way.

2.1.47.en: “Then shalt thou understand righteousness, and judgment, and equity; yea, every good path” [9].

2.1.48.en: By saying “then” he makes clear that God, who is the giver of all these gifts, when we respond to His gifts in a spirit of fear, grants us more understanding to perceive the law of His justice, truth and righteousness. It is as though wisdom enters our depths and enlightens our mind to perceive the will of God and the mysteries of His work.

2.2.0.en: 10 When wisdom entereth into thine heart, and knowledge is pleasant unto thy soul; 11 Discretion shall preserve thee, understanding shall keep thee: 12 To deliver thee from the way of the evil man, from the man that speaketh froward things; 13 Who leave the paths of uprightness, to walk in the ways of darkness; 14 Who rejoice to do evil, and delight in the frowardness of the wicked; 15 Whose ways are crooked, and they froward in their paths: 16 To deliver thee from the strange woman, even from the stranger which flattereth with her words; 17 Which forsaketh the guide of her youth, and forgetteth the covenant of her God. 18 For her house inclineth unto death, and her paths unto the dead. 19 None that go unto her return again, neither take they hold of the paths of life. 20 That thou mayest walk in the way of good men, and keep the paths of the righteous. 21 For the upright shall dwell in the land, and the perfect shall remain in it. 22 But the wicked shall be cut off from the earth, and the transgressors shall be rooted out of it.

2.2.1.en: When we listen in the fear of the Lord and ask Him for wisdom, knowledge and understanding, we enjoy these gifts in our depths, and they bring us the following gains:

2.3.s.en: First: delight of heart and inner happiness with satisfaction of mind

2.3.0.en: 10 When wisdom entereth into thine heart, and knowledge is pleasant unto thy soul; 11 Discretion shall preserve thee, understanding shall keep thee, “When wisdom entereth into thine heart, and knowledge is pleasant unto thy soul” [10].

2.3.1.en: As we incline our ears and cry with our mouths to God, the doors of our hearts open to receive divine wisdom and heavenly knowledge, and the commandments of God become no burden on the soul, and the yoke of Christ becomes light and sweet to the soul. The wisdom of God gives the soul joy, for in its reception of wisdom it finds union with Christ, the wisdom of God. This union is in itself a reward which the believer enjoys as a pledge of the heavenly reward. By divine wisdom the believer realizes that the aim of his life is to glorify God and to delight in Him.

2.4.s.en: Second: it delivers man from the paths of the wicked

2.4.0.en: 12 To deliver thee from the way of the evil man, from the man that speaketh froward things; 13 Who leave the paths of uprightness, to walk in the ways of darkness; 14 Who rejoice to do evil, and delight in the frowardness of the wicked; 15 Whose ways are crooked, and they froward in their paths:

2.4.1.en: “Discretion (discernment) shall preserve thee, understanding shall keep thee: to deliver thee from the way of the evil man, from the man that speaketh froward things; who leave the paths of uprightness, to walk in the ways of darkness” [11-13].

2.4.2.en: The Book of Proverbs teaches us that the people of God must be careful of two dangerous persons: the wicked man, and the foreign, corrupt woman.

2.4.3.en: A. The wicked man, who gives God his back and not his face, walks in his way by his own will, independent of God, feeling that he has no need of Him.

2.4.4.en: B. The adulterous woman, who upsets the balances, turning love into lusts, the body, God’s good creation, into an instrument of temporary pleasure, and the wide heart into selfishness! She puts on the mask of love, affection and cheerfulness, with lips dripping honey... and hides in her depths a poison deadly to the soul and a two-edged sword. She is a skilled hunter of foolish souls that bear the image of simplicity.

2.4.5.en: We see in the wicked man independence from God, and in the adulteress we see the corruption of the godly religious life. And as the Book of Revelation reveals to us that the kingdom of the Antichrist in the last ages will bear these two marks, it calls it “Babylon the Great, the mother of harlots.”

2.4.6.en: When wisdom has entered our hearts and become the object of our delight, we are not quickly deceived, but become watchful, able to avoid evil company and not to share in their evil conduct. In other words, wisdom leads us away from the way of the wicked and keeps us from their world and its enticements.

2.4.7.en: When wisdom reigns over the heart and controls the mind, she keeps them against every corruption, inner or outer. She draws from us every desire or inclination toward the way of darkness, since we realize that this way is neither comfortable nor safe.

2.4.8.en: We saw in the first chapter how the wicked find their delight in committing sin as in enticing others to commit it. The role of wisdom is the sanctification of the heart, the mind and the senses, so that she keeps the believer from fleshly lusts and temporal enticements, and the body and the soul together respond to the work of the Holy Spirit of God.

2.4.9.en: As we love divine wisdom we enjoy the mind or discernment which keeps the believer in his entirety and makes him able to take wise decisions that deliver him from the snares of the wicked. Thus the believer enjoys a life guarded on all sides, escaping the corruption that is in the world through lust.

2.4.10.en: “Who rejoice to do evil, and delight in the frowardness of the wicked.

2.4.11.en: Whose ways are crooked, and they froward in their paths” [14, 15].

2.4.12.en: Just as true believers rejoice in the living gifts of God, especially wisdom, knowledge and understanding, the wicked rejoice to do evil and delight in lying; but there is a difference between an inner joy that grows and is perfected in heaven, and a temporary one that turns into bitterness and sorrow.

2.4.13.en: While the way of the Lord is called straight and safe, the ways of the wicked are crooked, turning right and left from the straight way, full of tempests that shatter the soul.

2.5.s.en: Third: it keeps the believer from the snares of corrupt women

2.5.0.en: 16 To deliver thee from the strange woman, even from the stranger which flattereth with her words; 17 Which forsaketh the guide of her youth, and forgetteth the covenant of her God. 18 For her house inclineth unto death, and her paths unto the dead. 19 None that go unto her return again, neither take they hold of the paths of life.

2.5.1.en: “To deliver thee from the strange woman, even from the stranger which flattereth with her words; which forsaketh the guide (leader) of her youth, and forgetteth the covenant of her God” [16, 17].

2.5.2.en: By the foreign woman here is meant “the adulterous woman,” for God established a special law for the Israelite woman who practices prostitution, that she goes out automatically from Israel. It is as though “the foreign woman” here means the woman who came from the Gentiles practicing prostitution in the midst of Israel.

2.5.3.en: The flattering adulteress, hechelikah, is the one who offers sweet, gentle words. The Hebrew word means a slippery tongue that utters words like smooth oil. While the wicked try to entice others in a spirit of greed (Prov 1:11-19), the adulteresses try to entice them with fleshly lusts.

2.5.4.en: Though the adulteress is gentle in her sweet words, she is unfaithful to the one she loved and married in her youth; she forgets her covenant with him as she breaks her covenant with her God. Treachery and betrayal are in her nature even in her dealings with those nearest her, and even with God Himself. She pledged before God to marry her man, to leave her father’s house, and to submit in a spirit of faithfulness to the one she chose as her guide in her youth, who loves her and gives himself for her, and she submits to him in the Lord.

2.5.5.en: Here Solomon the Wise links married life with entering into a covenant with God, because marriage too is a covenant which God Himself establishes between the spouses, and He is a witness and judge of this holy covenant. St. Gregory of Nazianzus says, in his apology for his absence from the wedding celebration of Olympias and Nebridius: “Despite my illness I share your celebration, as I join the hands of the bride and groom together in the hands of God.”

2.6.0.en: “For her house sinketh (inclineth) unto death, and her paths unto the shades (the dead)” [18].

2.6.1.en: Although wisdom, like folly, has been symbolized by two women, it is clear that the speech here is not figurative, but means the adulterous woman, and the warning against her is clear and explicit, for she draws the one she entices into her house, that is, into eternal death, and walks with him in the ways of the dead, so that he smells no scent of life. This is what drives the true believer to flee from fornication, avoiding the adulterous woman whatever it costs him. While a man walks with her to her house, he is gradually descending toward eternal death, sharing with her the destructive way of sin. It is clear that the word “death” here does not mean the death to which all are subject but the eternal destiny.

2.6.2.en: “None that go unto her return again, neither take they hold of the paths of life” [16].

2.6.3.en: Fornication hastens a person, bringing him down to the way of death with no return. That is, whoever falls into the snares of fornication with a certain person finds it difficult, even impossible, to be delivered from it, unless the surpassing grace of God intervenes to support him and grant him the spirit of true repentance. Therefore many of the Fathers advise whoever falls into the sin of fornication not to meet the one with whom he fell, and not to go to the place where he committed the sin, declaring by this his sure desire and his response to the Holy Spirit of God, the giver of repentance, forgiveness and sanctification.

2.7.s.en: Fourth: it brings him into the way of the good

2.7.0.en: “That thou mayest walk in the way of good men, and keep the paths of the righteous.” [20].

2.7.1.en: The gifts of wisdom do not stop at the negatives, such as keeping from the ways of the wicked and delivering the believer from corrupt women, but present what is positive, which is bringing a person into the way of the good. For Christ, “the wisdom of God,” carries believers and brings them in to Himself as “the Way.” In Him the believer meets the holy men of God, and enters the company of the fathers, prophets, apostles and all the saints, and even shares the heavenly ones in their praise and love!

2.8.s.en: Fifth: he dwells safely in the land from which the wicked are rooted out

2.8.0.en: “For the upright shall dwell in the land, and the perfect shall remain in it.

2.8.1.en: But the wicked shall be cut off from the earth, and the transgressors shall be rooted out of it.” [21, 22].

2.8.2.en: Under the Mosaic Law the righteous received their reward, which was the safe land of Canaan. In the New Testament these gifts have become a symbol of heavenly spiritual gifts. The believer, though he does not receive a material land as a reward for his righteousness in Christ Jesus, sees all the earth, which belongs to the Lord and to His Christ, become his. He lives on it hidden in Christ, the King of heaven and earth, to reign with Him. He says with the Apostle Paul: “As having nothing, and yet possessing all things.” And he sings with David the prophet, saying: “Whatsoever he doeth shall prosper. The ungodly are not so: but are like the chaff which the wind driveth away... For the LORD knoweth the way of the righteous: but the way of the ungodly shall perish” (Ps 1:3-6).

2.8.3.en: In the epistle of St. Clement of Rome to the Corinthians he asks them to live in uprightness, in a spirit of unity and kindness so that they may enjoy this divine promise, for he says:

2.8.4.en: [Not a little harm comes upon us, but we come into great danger, if in impulsiveness we yield to the enticements of men who aim at stirring up strife and sedition in order to draw us away from what is good.

2.8.5.en: Let us be kind to one another after the pattern of the tenderness of the mercies and the kindness of our Creator, for it is written: “The good in heart shall dwell in the land, and the perfect shall remain in it, but the disobedient shall be cut off from the face of it.”]

2.8.6.en: Let me acquire You and carry You in my bosom
